entries.lesson_core_move: Compute \(p(t)=|x(t)|^2\) from a continuous-time signal \(x(t)\) and interpret it as the pointwise signal-size quantity that underlies energy and average-power calculations.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Instantaneous Power of a Signal
sections.learning_goal: Define instantaneous power as $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$ and explain that it measures signal size at each time.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the definition is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: No questions generated for this tutorial section.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Not applicable.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: State the definition $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$ and make clear that instantaneous power is the pointwise quantity later used for energy and average-power calculations.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a real-valued value such as $x(t_0)=3$ so the learner sees immediately that $p(t_0)=9$.
paragraph_plan: Introduce instantaneous power as the pointwise signal-size quantity attached to $x(t)$.
Give the definition $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$ and note that the magnitude is squared at each time.
Show a tiny numeric check at one time so the learner sees the square operation directly.
Close by connecting this quantity to later energy and average-power calculations without doing those calculations yet.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the explanation compact and definition-first. Do not add practice here; the next examples should immediately force substitution and then generalization.

sections.section_title: Computing Instantaneous Power at a Single Time
sections.learning_goal: Evaluate $p(t_0)=|x(t_0)|^2$ from a known signal value at one time.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; this is a one-time symbolic evaluation.

question_policy.answer_format: Five numeric answer choices; select the instantaneous power value at one time.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $x(5)=-6$, what is $p(5)$?
distractor_plan: Include the raw signal value as a sign-error distractor.
Include the absolute value without squaring as an incomplete distractor.
Include a doubled value or other simple arithmetic slip.
Include a square-of-time or square-of-coefficient mistake when the formula can tempt that error.
Include zero as an overcorrection distractor.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $x(2)=-4$, what is $p(2)$?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Evaluate the signal value at $t=2$, take its magnitude, square it, and conclude that $p(2)=16$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the definition to a single-time evaluation with a negative signal value so the learner sees that sign disappears after squaring.
solution_step_plan: Substitute the given time into $x(t)$ to get the signal value at that instant.
Take the magnitude of that value.
Square the magnitude to obtain the instantaneous power.
State the final value of $p(2)$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the evaluation time.
Change the signal value's sign and magnitude.
Use a simple numeric value or one-term expression for $x(t_0)$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this as a one-step substitution. Avoid introducing a full formula or piecewise structure yet.

sections.section_title: Computing an Instantaneous Power Signal from a Formula
sections.learning_goal: Convert a formula for $x(t)$ into the full power signal $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$ and simplify it.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the task is algebraic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; select the simplified expression for $p(t)$.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x(t)=3-2t$, what is $p(t)$?
distractor_plan: Leave the expression unsquared.
Square only one term instead of the whole magnitude.
Drop the absolute value and keep a sign-sensitive expression.
Expand incorrectly or omit a cross term.
Use $x(t)$ itself as the answer.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For $x(t)=2t-1$, find the instantaneous power signal $p(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $p(t)=|2t-1|^2=(2t-1)^2$ for this real-valued signal.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the single-time computation to a symbolic formula for all $t$ while keeping the same definition.
solution_step_plan: Write the definition $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$.
Substitute the given formula for $x(t)$.
Simplify the magnitude square for a real-valued expression.
State the simplified expression for $p(t)$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the linear coefficients or constant term in $x(t)$.
Use a simple sinusoid or constant signal instead of a line.
Include a negative factor so the square removes the sign.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the only new wrinkle as the transition from a single value to a full symbolic power function.

sections.section_title: Computing Instantaneous Power from Piecewise Signal Values
sections.learning_goal: Apply $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$ interval by interval when $x(t)$ is piecewise defined.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the piecewise data can stay textual.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; select the correct piecewise expression for $p(t)$.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=1$ for $0 \le t < 2$, $x(t)=-3$ for $2 \le t < 4$, and $x(t)=0$ otherwise, what is $p(t)$?
distractor_plan: Keep the original signal values instead of squaring them.
Square one interval correctly but not the other.
Reverse or alter the interval boundaries.
Leave the negative piece negative.
Drop the zero segment or fill it with the wrong constant.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For $x(t)=4$ for $0 \le t < 1$, $x(t)=-1$ for $1 \le t < 2$, and $x(t)=0$ otherwise, find the instantaneous power signal $p(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Compute $p(t)=16$ on $0 \le t < 1$, $p(t)=1$ on $1 \le t < 2$, and $p(t)=0$ otherwise.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the formula case to a piecewise signal so the same squaring rule is applied on each interval.
solution_step_plan: Apply the definition separately on each interval.
Square the magnitude of the constant value on each piece.
Carry the same interval boundaries into $p(t)$.
Check that a negative piece still gives positive power.
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of pieces.
Change one or more constant levels.
Include a zero segment or a different outside interval.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep interval bookkeeping explicit. The only new skill is carrying the magnitude square through piecewise values.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Zero and Larger Instantaneous Power Values
sections.learning_goal: Interpret zero and larger power values as statements about signal magnitude, not sign.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; interpretation stays symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five interpretation choices; select the statement that correctly relates power to magnitude.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $p(t_1)=0$ and $p(t_2)=16$, what are $x(t_1)$ and $|x(t_2)|$?
distractor_plan: Treat power as a signed quantity.
Treat zero power as merely small rather than exactly zero.
Use the wrong square root for the nonzero power.
Compare signs instead of magnitudes.
Claim that larger power means larger sign, not larger magnitude.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $p(t_1)=0$ and $p(t_2)=9$, what can you conclude about $x(t_1)$ and the magnitude of $x(t_2)$?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Conclude that $x(t_1)=0$ and $|x(t_2)|=3$, so the second signal has larger magnitude at that time.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from computing power to reading power back as a magnitude comparison and special-case interpretation.
solution_step_plan: Use $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$ to translate each power value back to a magnitude statement.
Recognize that zero power forces zero signal value at that time.
Take the square root of a positive power value to recover the signal magnitude.
Compare magnitudes without using the sign of $x(t)$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the specific power values.
Compare zero against a nonzero value.
Include same-power pairs that differ only by sign in the original signal.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section interpretive rather than computational. The goal is to read magnitude information out of power values.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert instantaneous signal power into signal energy by integrating \(|x(t)|^2\) over all time and interpreting finite or infinite totals as the signal-size basis for later energy, decaying-signal, and power classifications.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Signal Energy
sections.learning_goal: Define signal energy as the all-time integral of $|x(t)|^2$ and distinguish finite from infinite totals.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions for the tutorial step.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: State signal energy as the total accumulated size of $x(t)$ over time by integrating the instantaneous power $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a simple finite-duration constant pulse so the learner sees that a constant amplitude over a finite interval produces a finite energy value.
paragraph_plan: Open by framing signal energy as a total-size quantity, not an average, and connect that idea to the need for a time-integrated measure.
Introduce instantaneous power as $p(t)=|x(t)|^2$ and then define total energy as $E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^2\,dt$.
Explain that the same formula covers finite-energy and infinite-energy signals, so the value of the integral becomes the classification criterion.
Close with a one-line constant-pulse check that shows how a finite interval turns the definition into a concrete total.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial tight: define the quantity, show the formula once, and hand off immediately to examples that apply the definition.

sections.section_title: Converting Instantaneous Power into an Energy Integral
sections.learning_goal: Set up the total-energy integral from a given signal by squaring the magnitude and choosing the correct time limits.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: One correct symbolic energy integral among five choices.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which integral correctly represents the total energy of a rectangular pulse $x(t)=A$ for $0\le t<T$ and $0$ otherwise?
distractor_plan: Include a choice that forgets to square the amplitude and uses $A$ instead of $A^2$.
Include a choice that uses the wrong time limits, such as integrating over all time or over an interval that includes the zero region incorrectly.
Include a choice that uses $|x(t)|$ instead of $|x(t)|^2$.
Include a choice that evaluates a number too early instead of keeping the energy as an integral.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=3$ for $0\le t<2$ and $0$ otherwise, write the total energy as an integral of $|x(t)|^2$ and simplify the integrand.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to turn a piecewise-defined signal into the correct all-time energy integral by squaring the amplitude and restricting the bounds to the nonzero interval.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The tutorial defined energy; this example applies it to a simple finite-duration pulse and stops at the integral setup rather than completing the arithmetic.
solution_step_plan: Identify the interval where the signal is nonzero.
Square the constant amplitude to get the instantaneous power level.
Use the nonzero interval as the integration limits.
Write the simplified total-energy integral without evaluating it.
practice_variation_axes: Change the pulse amplitude while keeping the signal piecewise constant.
Change the support length and interval endpoints.
Change the notation from a piecewise definition to a step-function form.
Check that sign changes do not affect energy because of the magnitude square.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example focused on setting up the correct integral, not on finishing the definite integral.

sections.section_title: Evaluating a Finite Energy Integral
sections.learning_goal: Evaluate a finite-energy integral for a finite-duration signal and report the exact total.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: One exact scalar total-energy value among five choices.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the total energy of $x(t)=A$ for $0\le t<T$ and $0$ otherwise?
distractor_plan: Include a choice that forgets to square the amplitude and only multiplies by the duration.
Include a choice that multiplies the amplitude by itself but uses the wrong interval length.
Include a choice with a common arithmetic slip in the final scalar value.
Include a choice that reports the integral setup instead of the evaluated total.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute the total energy of $x(t)=2$ for $0\le t<3$ and $0$ otherwise.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Carry the setup through to the exact scalar value by integrating the constant power over its finite support.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example stopped at the energy integral; this one finishes the definite integral and reports the total.
solution_step_plan: Identify the finite interval where the signal is nonzero.
Square the amplitude to get the constant power level.
Integrate that constant over the support interval.
Simplify to the exact numeric energy.
practice_variation_axes: Change the amplitude to a different constant.
Change the pulse duration while preserving a finite support interval.
Change the endpoints to test whether the learner reads the interval correctly.
Use a signal written in step-function notation instead of piecewise form.

sections.handoff_notes: Show the full finite-interval calculation cleanly so later sections can contrast it with divergence.

sections.section_title: Identifying Infinite Signal Energy
sections.learning_goal: Determine when a signal's total-energy integral diverges and classify the energy as infinite.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: One finite-or-infinite classification among five choices.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Is the total energy of $x(t)=\cos(2\pi t)$ finite or infinite?
distractor_plan: Include a choice that treats bounded amplitude as proof of finite energy.
Include a choice that confuses energy with average power over one period.
Include a choice that uses the energy of one cycle instead of all time.
Include a choice that reports a finite numeric value despite the non-decaying signal.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Determine whether $x(t)=\cos(2\pi t)$ has finite or infinite energy, and justify the answer from the energy integral.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that a non-decaying periodic signal produces a divergent energy integral even though its amplitude stays bounded.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example had a finite support interval; this one removes that cutoff and shows that persistent nonzero power accumulates without bound.
solution_step_plan: Write the energy integral over all time.
Observe that the integrand is nonnegative and does not decay to zero.
Use the persistence of the signal to conclude that the integral diverges.
State the classification as infinite energy.
practice_variation_axes: Change the periodic waveform while keeping it non-decaying.
Use a constant signal instead of a sinusoid.
Change the frequency or phase without changing the infinite-energy conclusion.
Ask for the finite/infinite classification rather than the exact integral value.

sections.handoff_notes: Use a persistent non-decaying signal to make the divergence criterion explicit and avoid drifting into average-power discussion.

sections.section_title: Comparing Signals by Total Energy
sections.learning_goal: Compare two signals by computing and contrasting their total energy values.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: One correct comparison outcome among five choices.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which signal has the greater total energy: $x_1(t)=2$ for $0\le t<2$ or $x_2(t)=1$ for $0\le t<5$?
distractor_plan: Include a choice that compares only peak amplitude and ignores duration.
Include a choice that compares only duration and ignores amplitude.
Include a choice that forgets to square the amplitude before comparing totals.
Include a choice that makes a simple arithmetic mistake in one of the energies.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compare the total energies of $x_1(t)=2$ for $0\le t<2$ and $x_2(t)=1$ for $0\le t<5$, and state which is larger.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that total energy depends on both amplitude squared and duration, then use the computed totals to rank the signals.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example classified one signal as infinite energy; this one stays in the finite-energy regime and uses the totals to make a direct comparison.
solution_step_plan: Compute the energy of each signal from its constant amplitude and support length.
Compare the two numeric totals.
State which signal has larger energy or whether the energies are equal.
Tie the comparison back to the idea that energy measures total accumulated signal size.
practice_variation_axes: Change the amplitude-duration tradeoff so one signal is larger by a small margin.
Use two pulses with the same energy to test equality reasoning.
Swap which signal has the larger amplitude or longer duration.
Keep both signals finite-duration so the comparison stays within the energy classification.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the comparison strictly about total energy; do not drift into average power or periodic-signal classification.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the energy of a finite-duration continuous-time signal by using its support to set finite integration bounds, squaring its magnitude, and evaluating the resulting definite integral or piecewise sum.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Computing Energy of Finite-Duration Signals
sections.learning_goal: Build the idea that finite-duration energy is the integral of $|x(t)|^2$ over the signal's support, not over the entire time axis.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the tutorial is fully symbolic and should use support bounds and formulas only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this section.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions; this section is direct instruction only.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that when a signal is zero outside a finite support interval, its total energy is found by integrating $|x(t)|^2$ only over the nonzero interval.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A constant pulse $x(t)=A$ on $[a,b]$ and $0$ elsewhere.
paragraph_plan: Define a finite-duration signal and restate the energy formula from the earlier Signal Size work.
Show that the zero regions contribute nothing, so the integration bounds come from the support.
Work the constant-pulse base case to get $E=|A|^2(b-a)$.
Point out that later examples only change the signal shape inside the same support-limited procedure.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction brief and procedural. The writer should emphasize support-limited bounds first, then the squared-magnitude integral, then the constant-pulse base case.

sections.section_title: Computing Energy of a Constant Finite-Duration Signal
sections.learning_goal: Compute the energy of a constant finite-duration signal by squaring the constant magnitude and multiplying by the support length.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the worked example is a symbolic rectangular pulse.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this section.

question_policy.answer_format: Five numeric answer choices; select the total energy of the pulse.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the energy of a different constant pulse with a shifted support interval and a new amplitude, requiring the student to square the constant and use the interval length.
distractor_plan: Use the amplitude instead of the squared magnitude.
Use the wrong interval length by misreading the support endpoints.
Integrate over the whole real line instead of just the support.
Make a simple arithmetic error when multiplying the squared amplitude by the duration.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute the energy of $x(t)=2$ for $-1 \le t \le 2$, and $0$ otherwise.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $E=\int_{-1}^{2}|2|^2\,dt=12$ by identifying the support, squaring the constant magnitude, and multiplying by the duration.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first full worked example after the definition; it keeps the signal constant but shifts the support away from $t=0$ to force the learner to use the support bounds explicitly.
solution_step_plan: Identify the nonzero support interval from the signal definition.
Write the energy integral only over that support.
Square the constant magnitude and pull it outside the integral.
Evaluate the resulting length-times-height computation and state the numeric energy.
practice_variation_axes: Change the amplitude while keeping the signal constant on a finite interval.
Shift the support interval to a different location on the time axis.
Change the interval length so the student must recompute the duration.
Change the numeric result so the student cannot rely on a memorized answer.

sections.handoff_notes: The answer choices should be scalar numeric values. Keep the prompt as a single rectangular pulse and do not add an image.

sections.section_title: Computing Energy of a Nonconstant Finite-Duration Signal
sections.learning_goal: Compute the energy of a nonconstant finite-duration signal by squaring the time-varying formula and evaluating the definite integral over its support.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the signal is given as a simple formula on a finite interval.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this section.

question_policy.answer_format: Five numeric answer choices; select the exact energy value, often a fraction.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the energy of a different simple polynomial or ramp signal on a finite interval, so the student must square the formula and integrate the resulting polynomial.
distractor_plan: Integrate $x(t)$ instead of $|x(t)|^2$.
Forget to square the coefficient in front of the time variable.
Use the wrong antiderivative or evaluate it incorrectly.
Use the wrong support bounds from the signal definition.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute the energy of $x(t)=2t$ for $0 \le t \le 1$, and $0$ otherwise.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $E=\int_0^1 |2t|^2\,dt=\frac{4}{3}$ by squaring the formula, integrating the resulting polynomial, and evaluating it on the support.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds the first time-varying formula: the support-limited setup is unchanged, but the integrand is no longer constant.
solution_step_plan: Identify the support interval and write the energy integral over that interval only.
Square the signal formula inside the integrand.
Integrate the resulting polynomial.
Evaluate the antiderivative at the endpoints and simplify the fraction.
practice_variation_axes: Change the coefficient on $t$.
Use a different simple power such as $t^2$ while keeping the support finite.
Shift the support interval to a different location.
Keep the same support length but alter the function so the student must re-integrate.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the algebra light and the support explicit. The example should stay on one smooth formula so the only new challenge is squaring and integrating a nonconstant signal.

sections.section_title: Computing Energy of a Piecewise Finite-Duration Signal
sections.learning_goal: Compute the energy of a piecewise finite-duration signal by splitting the support at each breakpoint, integrating $|x(t)|^2$ on each piece, and summing the results.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the signal is defined piecewise by formulas and breakpoints.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this section.

question_policy.answer_format: Five numeric answer choices; select the summed energy from the piecewise intervals.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the energy of a different two-piece finite-duration signal with a new breakpoint and new constant values, so the student must split the integral and add the pieces.
distractor_plan: Square only one piece or only one amplitude.
Add the raw amplitudes instead of the energies from each interval.
Merge the intervals and integrate across a breakpoint incorrectly.
Drop one active piece or miss a gap between pieces.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute the energy of $x(t)=1$ for $0 \le t < 1$, $x(t)=2$ for $1 \le t \le 3$, and $0$ otherwise.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the energy is the sum of the two active intervals, $E=\int_0^1 1^2\,dt+\int_1^3 2^2\,dt=9$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The new wrinkle is that the signal has two nonzero pieces, so the learner must split the integral at an internal breakpoint instead of using one interval.
solution_step_plan: Read the piecewise definition and mark each active interval.
Square each piece on its own interval.
Write one integral per interval.
Evaluate each piece and add the results.
practice_variation_axes: Change the breakpoint locations.
Change the amplitudes on each piece.
Add or remove a zero gap between active pieces.
Vary the number of pieces while keeping each piece simple.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the breakpoints explicit and make the sum of interval energies visible. The main skill is splitting one finite-duration signal into manageable pieces and recombining the results.

sections.section_title: Computing Energy of a Finite-Duration Signal from a Graph
sections.learning_goal: Read a finite-duration signal from its graph, translate the visible support and segments into integrals, and compute the energy from the plotted shape.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean graph of a finite-duration signal on Cartesian axes: zero outside a compact interval, with a simple triangular or trapezoidal pulse on the support and labeled breakpoints and amplitudes.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a minimal black-and-white math graph with clear numeric labels. The worked example and follow-up questions should use graph data only; the practice graphs should vary the support endpoints and heights while staying simple enough to integrate by hand.

question_policy.answer_format: Five numeric answer choices; the graph supplies the signal shape and the student chooses the correct total energy.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Ask for the energy of a different finite-duration signal shown only by a graph, with similarly simple piecewise-linear segments and compact support.
distractor_plan: Read the graph's height or breakpoints incorrectly.
Compute area under the graph instead of energy.
Square only one side of the graph and forget the other segment.
Use the wrong support interval or miss an endpoint.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute the energy of the finite-duration signal shown in the graph: a triangular pulse that is zero outside $0 \le t \le 2$, rises linearly from $(0,0)$ to $(1,2)$, and falls linearly back to $(2,0)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Translate the graph into two linear pieces, square each piece, integrate over $[0,1]$ and $[1,2]$, and add the results to get the total energy.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The signal is now given visually, so the first job is to read support, breakpoints, and heights from the graph before applying the same support-limited energy procedure.
solution_step_plan: Read the support endpoints and the key vertex values directly from the graph.
Write the signal as piecewise formulas on each linear segment.
Square each segment and integrate over its own subinterval.
Add the subinterval energies and simplify the numeric result.
practice_variation_axes: Change the graph's peak height.
Change the support width or shift the graph along the time axis.
Use a graph with a different piecewise-linear shape but the same overall finite-duration setup.
Vary the number of linear segments while keeping the graph simple enough for hand integration.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the only image-driven section in the lesson. The graph should be the problem data, not decoration, and the follow-up questions should reuse the same skill with new graph images.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute total energy for decaying continuous-time signals by squaring the signal magnitude, setting the correct semi-infinite integration limits, and evaluating the resulting convergent improper integral.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Computing Energy of Decaying Signals
sections.learning_goal: Teach students to compute the total energy of a decaying signal by integrating $|x(t)|^2$ over its support and treating the semi-infinite tail as an improper integral.

question_policy.answer_format: Not applicable; no questions are generated for this tutorial step.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Not applicable; this section is a tutorial step.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that the energy of a decaying continuous-time signal is still $E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^2\,dt$, but the integral collapses to the signal's semi-infinite support and must be evaluated as an improper integral.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use $x(t)=e^{-at}u(t)$ with $a>0$ as the base case, so the learner only has to set up $E=\int_0^\infty e^{-2at}\,dt$ and evaluate the convergent tail.
paragraph_plan: Connect the lesson to finite-duration energy: same definition, but the signal now lives on $[0,\infty)$ instead of a finite interval.
Introduce the base signal $x(t)=e^{-at}u(t)$ and identify the support from the unit step.
Square the magnitude and collapse the full-time integral to $\int_0^\infty e^{-2at}\,dt$.
Evaluate the improper integral, making the convergence condition $a>0$ explicit.
Close by generalizing the pattern to shifted start times and amplitude factors.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not applicable; this section is a tutorial step.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Not applicable.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Not applicable.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the exposition short and tightly scaffolded: this is the first time the learner sees a convergent improper energy integral, so stress support, lower limit, and convergence before any algebraic shortcuts.

sections.section_title: Energy of a One-Sided Decaying Exponential
sections.learning_goal: Compute the energy of a one-sided decaying exponential by squaring the signal, integrating on $[0,\infty)$, and simplifying the convergent improper integral.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct total energy value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Compute the total energy of $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ by writing the improper integral over the support and evaluating it.
distractor_plan: Use $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}$ or the wrong lower limit instead of the support $[0,\infty)$.
Forget to square the signal magnitude, which would miss the exponent doubling.
Treat the signal as infinite-energy simply because it extends forever.
Make the factor-of-two error in the denominator after integration.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is an example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the total energy of $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $E=\int_0^\infty e^{-2t}\,dt=\frac{1}{2}$ and that the result is finite because the exponential tail decays.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the simplest concrete version of the tutorial base case: the learner now carries out the complete computation with a specific decay rate.
solution_step_plan: Read the support from $u(t)$ and set up $E=\int_0^\infty |e^{-t}|^2\,dt$.
Square the magnitude to get $e^{-2t}$.
Evaluate the improper integral over $[0,\infty)$.
Simplify the result to $\frac{1}{2}$ and note that the integral converges.
practice_variation_axes: Change the decay constant while keeping the same one-sided support.
Keep the same support but ask for the energy as a decimal or simplified fraction.
Ask the learner to identify the correct lower limit before integrating.

sections.handoff_notes: The later question set should stay purely symbolic and should not introduce a shift yet; the only new move here is the improper integral on $[0,\infty)$.

sections.section_title: Energy of a Scaled Decaying Exponential
sections.learning_goal: Apply amplitude scaling to a decaying-exponential energy calculation by integrating $|A e^{-at}u(t)|^2$ over $[0,\infty)$.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct total energy value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Compute the total energy of $x(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)$ by squaring the amplitude and integrating over the support.
distractor_plan: Forget to square the amplitude and therefore undercount the energy.
Use the wrong lower limit instead of $0$.
Drop the factor of 2 in the exponential after squaring.
Treat the scaling as changing the support rather than only the magnitude.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is an example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the total energy of $x(t)=3e^{-t}u(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the amplitude contributes a factor of $9$ after squaring, so the energy is $E=9\int_0^\infty e^{-2t}\,dt=\frac{9}{2}$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The support and decay shape are the same as the previous example, but the learner must carry an amplitude scale through the squaring step.
solution_step_plan: Identify support $t\ge 0$ and write the energy integral.
Square the amplitude to get $9e^{-2t}$.
Evaluate the improper integral on $[0,\infty)$.
Simplify the result and confirm that the energy is finite.
practice_variation_axes: Change the amplitude while keeping the same one-sided exponential shape.
Keep the support at $t\ge 0$ so the only new wrinkle is amplitude scaling.
Ask for the intermediate squared signal before asking for the final energy.

sections.handoff_notes: Highlight amplitude-squared scaling before evaluation. Do not add a time shift here; the point is to isolate the effect of the coefficient in front of the exponential.

sections.section_title: Energy of a Decaying Exponential with a Nonzero Start Time
sections.learning_goal: Set the lower integration limit from a nonzero start time and compute the energy of a shifted decaying exponential on $[t_0,\infty)$.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct total energy value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Compute the total energy of $x(t)=e^{-(t-3)}u(t-3)$ by setting the lower bound from the start time and evaluating the improper integral.
distractor_plan: Integrate from $0$ instead of the shifted start time.
Forget that the unit step changes the support, not the decay rate.
Drop the square on the exponential and keep $e^{-(t-3)}$ instead of $e^{-2(t-3)}$ after squaring.
Treat the shift as changing the energy value rather than just the integration bounds.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is an example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find the total energy of $x(t)=e^{-(t-3)}u(t-3)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the support starts at $t=3$, so the energy is $E=\int_3^\infty e^{-2(t-3)}\,dt=\frac{1}{2}$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The signal is still a one-sided decaying exponential, but the nonzero start time forces the learner to move the lower limit from $0$ to $3$.
solution_step_plan: Read the support from $u(t-3)$ and set up the integral from $3$ to $\infty$.
Square the signal magnitude and simplify the integrand.
Optionally shift variables with $\tau=t-3$ to match the tutorial base case.
Evaluate the improper integral and state the finite energy.
practice_variation_axes: Change the start time $t_0$ while keeping the decay rate fixed.
Ask for the support interval before asking for the energy.
Swap the order of the shift and amplitude so the learner must still set the correct bounds.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the focus on lower bounds and support. The key misconception to guard against is treating a time shift as if it changes the total energy itself.

sections.section_title: Checking Convergence of a Decaying-Signal Energy Integral
sections.learning_goal: Check whether a decaying-signal energy integral converges before evaluating it, and then compute the finite energy when the decay parameter is positive.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; one correct convergence statement or energy expression.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Determine whether $x(t)=e^{-bt}u(t)$ has finite energy, and if so find it.
distractor_plan: Use $a<0$ or $a\le 0$ as if the integral still converged.
Return $\frac{1}{a}$ instead of $\frac{1}{2a}$ after squaring.
Claim the energy is infinite simply because the signal lasts for infinite time.
Forget to inspect the sign of the exponent after squaring.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not applicable; this section is an example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For which values of $a$ does $x(t)=e^{-at}u(t)$ have finite energy, and what is the energy when it converges?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $E=\int_0^\infty e^{-2at}\,dt$ converges only when $a>0$, and that in that case $E=\frac{1}{2a}$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Unlike the earlier examples, this one makes the learner decide convergence from a symbolic parameter instead of just evaluating a concrete improper integral.
solution_step_plan: Square the signal and write the energy integral on $[0,\infty)$.
Check the sign of the decay rate in the exponent to decide convergence.
Evaluate the integral symbolically for the convergent case $a>0$.
State that the energy is infinite or undefined when $a\le 0$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the decay parameter and ask for the convergence condition first.
Use a parameterized decay law whose sign must be simplified before deciding convergence.
Include one non-decaying or growing distractor case to test whether the learner recognizes divergence.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the most abstract example in the lesson. Make convergence the first decision point, then compute only after the learner has established $a>0$.

paragraph_plan: State the average-power definition and name the quantity as sustained signal size.

Use the constant-signal base case to show that a nonzero steady signal keeps the same average power.

sections.section_title: Computing Average Power of a Constant Signal
sections.learning_goal: Compute average signal power for a constant signal by pulling $|A|^2$ through the long-time average.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the computation is symbolic-only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: single symbolic expression for $P_{\text{avg}}$
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the average signal power of the constant signal $x(t)=A$?
distractor_plan: Use $A$ instead of $|A|^2$.
Use the finite-window energy $2T|A|^2$ instead of the average.
Drop the magnitude and square the signed constant incorrectly.
Choose zero by confusing a constant signal with a finite-duration signal.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute the average signal power of the constant signal $x(t)=A$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the symmetric long-time average of a constant is the constant itself, so the average power is $|A|^2$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the simplest direct application of the definition: the signal never changes in time, so the only job is to average a constant magnitude-squared value.
solution_step_plan: Write the average-power limit for $x(t)=A$.
Substitute $|x(t)|^2=|A|^2$ into the integral.
Evaluate the integral over $[-T,T]$ as $2T|A|^2$.
Divide by $2T$ and take the limit to get $|A|^2$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the constant amplitude from symbolic to numeric.
Use a complex constant with the same magnitude.
Vary the notation but keep the signal time-invariant.

sections.handoff_notes: Mirror the definition exactly; use one clean symbolic computation and one or two parameter variations.

sections.section_title: Computing Zero Average Power for a Finite-Duration Signal
sections.learning_goal: Show that a finite-duration signal has zero average power because its nonzero contribution is diluted by the growing averaging window.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the computation is symbolic-only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: single symbolic value
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the average signal power of the finite-duration pulse $x(t)=A$ for $|t|\le T_0$ and $x(t)=0$ otherwise?
distractor_plan: Return the finite energy $2T_0|A|^2$ instead of the average.
Return $|A|^2$ by averaging only over the support interval.
Confuse the result with a duration-dependent quantity.
Choose infinity from the growing integration window.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute the average signal power of the finite-duration pulse $x(t)=A$ for $|t|\le T_0$ and $x(t)=0$ otherwise.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the integral stays finite while the $2T$ normalization grows without bound, so the average power is $0$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Unlike the constant signal, this signal is nonzero only on a bounded interval, so the long-time average collapses to zero even though the pulse has finite energy.
solution_step_plan: Write the average-power limit for the pulse.
Restrict the integral to the finite support interval.
Evaluate the fixed finite integral as $2T_0|A|^2$.
Divide by $2T$ and take $T \to \infty$ to get $0$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the pulse width.
Shift the finite-duration support.
Swap in another bounded-support waveform.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the support interval explicit so the later writer can show the numerator is fixed while the denominator grows.

sections.section_title: Computing Average Power of a Decaying Signal
sections.learning_goal: Compute average signal power for a decaying signal and see that decay can still force the long-time average to zero.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the computation is symbolic-only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: single symbolic value
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the average signal power of $x(t)=e^{-a|t|}$ for $a>0$?
distractor_plan: Return the finite integral $1/a$ instead of the averaged limit.
Return $1/(2a)$ from missing the symmetry factor.
Return the peak power $1$ instead of the long-time average.
Return a nonzero value by stopping before the limit.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute the average signal power of the decaying signal $x(t)=e^{-a|t|}$ with $a>0$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Evaluate the symmetric average of $e^{-2a|t|}$ and show that the result tends to $0$ as the averaging window grows.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This signal is not compactly supported, but its decay still keeps the squared-magnitude integral bounded, so the average power vanishes after division by the widening window.
solution_step_plan: Write the symmetric average-power limit.
Use even symmetry to reduce the integral to $2\int_0^T e^{-2at}\,dt$.
Evaluate the integral exactly.
Divide by $2T$ and let $T \to \infty$ to obtain $0$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the decay rate $a$.
Switch between two-sided and one-sided decay.
Use another decaying envelope with finite energy.

sections.handoff_notes: Use the same signal family as the worked example, but vary the decay rate or the side on which the decay occurs.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing Average Power from Total Energy
sections.learning_goal: Distinguish average signal power from total energy by computing both quantities for a finite-energy decaying signal.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the comparison is symbolic-only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image.

question_policy.answer_format: classification statement comparing energy and average power
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which statement correctly compares the total energy and average signal power of $x(t)=e^{-a|t|}$ for $a>0$?
distractor_plan: Confuse energy with average power and assign the same finite value to both.
Claim the average power is $1/a$ because the energy integral is finite.
Claim both quantities are zero.
Claim the signal is a power signal because it lasts forever.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the signal $x(t)=e^{-a|t|}$ with $a>0$, compute its total energy and its average signal power, then state which quantity is finite.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the total energy is finite while the average power is zero, so energy and average power capture different signal-size notions.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This final example reuses the decaying signal but compares the finite total-energy integral with the long-time average limit on the same signal.
solution_step_plan: Compute total energy $E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^2\,dt$ and get a finite constant.
Compute average power with the symmetric long-time average.
Show the average power tends to $0$ because the energy is finite.
State the conceptual distinction: finite total accumulation versus sustained size.
practice_variation_axes: Change the decay rate.
Swap in a different finite-energy signal.
Ask for the energy-versus-power classification instead of a direct numeric computation.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the contrast explicit: finite total energy is not the same thing as sustained average power.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the power of a periodic continuous-time signal by converting the average-power limit into \(P=\frac{1}{T_0}\int_{t_0}^{t_0+T_0}|x(t)|^2\,dt\) over any fundamental period.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Power of Periodic Signals
sections.learning_goal: Define periodic signal power as the average of $|x(t)|^2$ over one full period and explain why any fundamental-period interval gives the same result.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: No questions generated for this tutorial section.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Not applicable.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that the average-power limit for a periodic signal collapses to one full-period average, so the learner can compute power from any interval of length $T_0$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a signal that repeats the same constant level over each period so the repeated-interval averaging idea is obvious.
paragraph_plan: Recall the average-power definition from the previous lesson and state the periodic-signal goal.
Break a long interval into repeated copies of one fundamental period.
Cancel the repeated copies and isolate the one-period average.
Note that the starting point $t_0$ does not matter as long as the interval length is $T_0$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the explanation anchored to repetition over one full period. Later sections should not re-derive the limit unless they need to show why the shortcut works.

sections.section_title: Converting Average Power to a One-Period Integral
sections.learning_goal: Rewrite the average-power limit for a periodic signal as an integral over one fundamental period.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; select the correct one-period power expression.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which expression correctly rewrites the average power of a $T_0$-periodic signal in terms of one fundamental period?
distractor_plan: Include a choice that keeps the long-interval limit but does not collapse it to one period.
Include a choice that drops the $1/T_0$ factor.
Include a choice that uses $|x(t)|$ instead of $|x(t)|^2$.
Include a choice whose bounds do not span exactly one full period.
Include a choice that averages the amplitude rather than the squared magnitude.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For a $T_0$-periodic signal $x(t)$, show how the average-power limit reduces to a one-period integral over $[t_0,t_0+T_0]$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use periodic repetition to replace the long-interval average-power limit with the one-period formula $P=\frac{1}{T_0}\int_{t_0}^{t_0+T_0}|x(t)|^2\,dt$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the general periodic-power idea to the algebraic collapse of the limit itself, without evaluating a specific signal yet.
solution_step_plan: Identify the fundamental period and the repeated waveform.
Partition the long interval into whole periods.
Replace each repeated block with the same one-period integral.
Cancel the repetition count and state the one-period formula.
practice_variation_axes: Change the period length.
Shift the integration bounds to $[t_0,t_0+T_0]$.
Change the waveform over one period without changing the algebraic collapse.
Ask for the equivalent integral expression rather than a numeric value.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this step purely as the algebraic collapse of the average-power limit. Do not evaluate a specific periodic waveform yet.

sections.section_title: Computing Power from a Given Fundamental Period
sections.learning_goal: Evaluate the one-period integral for a simple periodic waveform when the fundamental period is given.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices; select the correct power value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the power of the periodic signal $x(t)=2$ for $0\le t<\tfrac{T_0}{2}$ and $0$ for $\tfrac{T_0}{2}\le t<T_0$, repeated every $T_0$?
distractor_plan: Include a choice that forgets to square the amplitude.
Include a choice that uses the full period length instead of the active subinterval length.
Include a choice that divides by the active subinterval length instead of $T_0$.
Include a choice that treats the zero segment as if it contributed nonzero power.
Include a choice with a simple arithmetic slip in the final scalar value.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Compute the power of the periodic signal $x(t)=2$ for $0\le t<\tfrac{T_0}{2}$ and $0$ for $\tfrac{T_0}{2}\le t<T_0$, repeated every $T_0$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use $P=\frac{1}{T_0}\int_0^{T_0}|x(t)|^2\,dt$ to get $P=2$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keeps the same one-period formula but now evaluates it on a waveform with a simple active-and-zero pattern.
solution_step_plan: Write the one-period power formula.
Square the nonzero amplitude on its interval.
Integrate over the active and zero subintervals.
Divide by $T_0$ and simplify.
practice_variation_axes: Change the active-level amplitude.
Change the active-duty fraction of the period.
Use a different period length.
Include a negative level so the square removes the sign.

sections.handoff_notes: Use a waveform simple enough that the only new work is integrating over one period. Keep the arithmetic clean and direct.

sections.section_title: Choosing Convenient Bounds Over One Period

Split the integral at the breakpoint.

sections.section_title: Computing Power of a Piecewise Periodic Signal

sections.section_title: Introduction to Energy Signals vs. Power Signals
sections.learning_goal: Teach the learner to classify a continuous-time signal by computing total energy and time-average power and comparing them to the finite-energy and finite-nonzero-power criteria.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; this step is symbolic and formula-driven.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Give the learner the minimal rule set for deciding whether a signal is an energy signal, a power signal, or neither from its total energy and time-average power.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a finite-duration nonzero pulse so $E_x$ is finite and nonzero while $P_x=0$; that anchors the energy-signal criterion before the harder cases.
paragraph_plan: State the classification goal up front: signal size is judged by total energy and time-average power, not by visual shape alone.
Define $E_x$ and $P_x$ with compact display math and explain that each quantity measures a different notion of signal size.
State the decision rule: $0<E_x<\infty$ means energy signal, $0<P_x<\infty$ means power signal, and anything else is neither.
Preview that the worked examples will test one finite-energy case, one finite-power case, and two neither cases.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction short and direct; no practice questions or visual support are needed here.

sections.section_title: Classifying Signals with Finite Nonzero Energy
sections.learning_goal: Show that a decaying transient can have finite nonzero total energy and zero average power, so it is an energy signal.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; keep the worked example symbolic and low load.

question_policy.answer_format: signal classification label
question_policy.practice_question_model: Classify $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ as an energy signal, a power signal, or neither by computing total energy and average power.
distractor_plan: Use `power signal` as the main distractor for the misconception that any signal with infinite support must be a power signal.
Use `neither` for the misconception that a decaying signal cannot have finite energy.
Use `both energy and power` only as a deliberate foil for the mistaken belief that the categories overlap.
Use `zero-power signal` if the generator needs a label-style trap for confusing zero average power with failure to classify.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Classify $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ as an energy signal, a power signal, or neither by computing total energy and average power.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Compute $E_x$ as finite and nonzero, show that $P_x=0$, and conclude that the signal is an energy signal.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: First concrete computation after the tutorial; replaces the abstract rule with a one-sided decaying signal that still has infinite support.
solution_step_plan: Write the energy integral $E_x=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|^2\,dt$ for the given signal.
Evaluate the integral and note that the result is finite and nonzero.
Compute or reason that $P_x=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}|x(t)|^2\,dt=0$.
Conclude that the signal is an energy signal, not a power signal.
practice_variation_axes: Decay rate
Amplitude scaling
Time shift
Other finite-energy transients with infinite support

sections.section_title: Classifying Signals with Finite Nonzero Average Power

question_policy.practice_question_model: Classify $x(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t)$ as an energy signal, a power signal, or neither by computing total energy and average power.

Use `both energy and power` only if the later generator needs an impossible category trap.

sections.section_title: Classifying Signals with Infinite Energy and Infinite Average Power
sections.learning_goal: Show that a growing signal can make both energy and average power diverge, so it is classified as neither.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the example should stay entirely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: signal classification label
question_policy.practice_question_model: Classify $x(t)=t\,u(t)$ as an energy signal, a power signal, or neither by computing total energy and average power.
distractor_plan: Use `energy signal` for the misconception that the signal is finite on every bounded interval, so energy must be finite.
Use `power signal` for the misconception that normalization by $2T$ keeps every growing signal finite.
Use `zero-power signal` as a foil for learners who focus only on the large-$T$ averaging step.
Use `both energy and power` only if the later generator needs a deliberately impossible category.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Classify $x(t)=t\,u(t)$ as an energy signal, a power signal, or neither by computing total energy and average power.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that both $E_x$ and $P_x$ diverge, so the signal is neither an energy signal nor a power signal.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from finite-power periodic behavior to a growing signal whose squared magnitude keeps increasing, so both integrals blow up.
solution_step_plan: Set up $E_x$ and show that the integral of $|t|^2$ on $[0,\infty)$ diverges.
Set up $P_x$ and show that the normalized integral grows without bound as $T\to\infty$.
Use both divergences to rule out energy and power signal classes.
Conclude neither.

sections.section_title: Classifying Signals with Infinite Energy and Zero Average Power
sections.learning_goal: Show that a slowly decaying signal can still have infinite total energy even when its average power tends to zero, so it is classified as neither.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the classification depends only on symbolic integration.

question_policy.answer_format: signal classification label
question_policy.practice_question_model: Classify $x(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}}u(t)$ as an energy signal, a power signal, or neither by computing total energy and average power.
distractor_plan: Use `energy signal` for the misconception that decay alone guarantees finite energy.
Use `power signal` for the misconception that zero average power still qualifies as a power signal.
Use `zero-power signal` as a foil for learners who conflate zero average power with the energy class.
Use `both energy and power` only if the later generator needs a deliberately impossible category.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Classify $x(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}}u(t)$ as an energy signal, a power signal, or neither by computing total energy and average power.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that $E_x$ diverges logarithmically while $P_x$ tends to zero, so the signal is neither.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keeps the neither classification but changes the failure mode from unbounded growth to slow decay: the average power vanishes even though total energy still diverges.
solution_step_plan: Set up $E_x$ and show that the integral of $1/(t+1)$ diverges.
Compute $P_x$ from the average of $1/(t+1)$ over $[0,T]$.
Show the power limit goes to zero even though the energy diverges.
Conclude neither because finite energy is required for an energy signal and finite nonzero average power is required for a power signal.
practice_variation_axes: Decay exponent
Turn-on shift
Amplitude scaling
Other slow-decay tails

sections.handoff_notes: Symbolic-only neither-case example; the later question generator should keep the same slow-decay logic and make sure the zero-average-power trap does not override the infinite-energy conclusion.
